title: Zeuthen_strategy
summary:
The Zeuthen strategy is a negotiation strategy used by some artificial agents in cognitive science, designed to measure the willingness to risk conflict. An agent will be more willing to risk conflict if it does not have much to lose in case that the negotiation fails. The strategy originates from the work of Danish economist Frederik Zeuthen, who introduced it in 1930 in his book Problems of Monopoly and Economic Warfare.

At its core, the strategy revolves around calculating each agent's risk of conflict in each bargaining round, defined as the ratio of the utility loss from fully conceding to the opponent's demand versus the utility loss from impasse. The strategy addresses three key questions: any agent should start with its most preferred deal because it has the highest utility; the agent with the smallest risk value concedes because it profits most from avoiding conflict; and the conceding agent should concede just enough to raise its risk value just above that of the other agent.

In Zeuthen's book, he proposed a solution to the bargaining problem which Harsanyi later showed is equivalent to Nash's bargaining solution. In his 1956 paper, John C. Harsanyi reformulated Zeuthen's procedure in modern utility terms and demonstrated its equivalence to the Nash bargaining solution under complete information and symmetric risk neutrality.

The design of the Zeuthen strategy is influenced by strong assumptions about agents' capabilities, values, rationality and common knowledge, with a fairly simple interaction protocol that only allows agents to either make proposed deals or concede. If both agents use Zeuthen strategies, they will agree on an outcome, and given assumptions about the agents involved, the strategy becomes deterministic, meaning strategy designers have no room for deviating without risking a worse outcome.
